w: Fremantle's first permanent building, built in late 1830 and opened in 1831 on Arthur Head - the second-oldest surviving European building in Western Australia, after the Wiebbe Hayes Stone Fort on West Wallabi Island. The rise it stands on was once known as Gaol Hill.
s: WA's second-oldest building, on a rise called Gaol Hill
_facts: First permanent building in the Swan River Colony, built 1830-31
Second-oldest surviving European building in Western Australia
Located at Arthur Head, a site once called Gaol Hill

w: Built in 1906 at the entrance to Fremantle Harbour, designed by engineer C.Y. O'Connor, who also built the harbour itself. The 15-metre red cast-iron tower throws an occulting light visible for 18 kilometres. Its green twin on the south mole is the last of its kind, and the spot is a favourite for fishing.
s: O'Connor's red 1906 lighthouse at the harbour mouth
_facts: Began operation 1906 at the entrance to Fremantle Harbour
Designed by engineer C.Y. O'Connor, builder of the harbour
15-metre cast-iron tower, light visible 18km
Green-painted twin on the south mole - the last of their type

w: An Oberon-class submarine built in Scotland for the Royal Australian Navy, in service from 1969 to 1995. Ovens was the first RAN submarine to fire an armed Mark 48 torpedo, sinking the target ship Colac. Decommissioned in 1995, she's preserved as a museum ship at the WA Maritime Museum.
s: Decommissioned RAN submarine, now a museum ship
_facts: Oberon-class submarine, one of six built for the RAN by Scotts Shipbuilding
In service 1969-1995
First RAN submarine to fire an armed Mark 48 torpedo, sinking target ship Colac
Preserved as a museum ship at the WA Maritime Museum

w: Formerly Kings Square, this town square has been Fremantle's civic heart since colonial days - Saint John's Church of England has stood here since 1843, and Fremantle Town Hall since 1887. High Street once ran straight through it, until that stretch was closed off in the 1960s.
s: Fremantle's old civic square, renamed Walyalup Koort
_facts: Formerly known as Kings Square
Site of St John's Church of England since 1843 and Fremantle Town Hall since 1887
High Street once cut through the square; closed off in the 1960s

w: A merchant complex on Henry Street unified in 1899 behind an ornamental stucco facade, with parts possibly dating to the 1840s. W D Moore traded flour, wine and mining gear by mail order. The Moore family sold up in 1956; the City of Fremantle bought and restored the complex in 1985-86 for the America's Cup defence.
s: 1890s merchant warehouse restored for the America's Cup
_facts: Unified in 1899 behind a stucco facade; oldest part possibly from the 1840s
W D Moore traded flour, wine, mining equipment and more, including by mail order
Sold to a transport company in 1956; bought and restored by the City of Fremantle 1985-86 for the America's Cup defence

w: Designed by Hillson Beasley of the Public Works Department and opened in 1907 on Market Street. It was renovated for WA's 1929 centenary and again for the 1987 America's Cup challenge. A storm in August 2022 brought the ceiling down, and postal operations moved out to 22 Queen Street while repairs continue.
s: 1907 post office, patched up after a 2022 ceiling collapse
_facts: Designed by Hillson Beasley, opened 1907
Renovated in 1929 for WA's centenary and 1987 for the America's Cup
Ceiling collapsed after an August 2022 storm; operations moved to 22 Queen Street

w: Built in 1908 to house the Customs Department of Western Australia, this is one of only a handful of Customs Houses still standing in the state - the others are in Albany, Broome, Cossack and Geraldton.
s: One of only five surviving WA Customs Houses
_facts: Built in 1908 for the Customs Department of Western Australia
One of only a handful of extant Customs Houses in WA, alongside Albany, Broome, Cossack and Geraldton

w: A three-storey Federation Free Classic hotel at 80 High Street, registered on the Register of the National Estate in 1978. These days the old pub trades as the Sundancers Backpackers Hostel rather than pulling beers.
s: Federation-era pub on High Street, now a hostel
_facts: Three-storey Federation Free Classic building at 80 High Street
Registered on the Register of the National Estate in 1978
Now operates as Sundancers Backpackers Hostel

w: Built for the Bank of New South Wales in 1899, during the gold-boom years when Fremantle was WA's trading hub. A single-storey Federation Free Classical building with an elaborate stucco facade. The bank operated here until 1926, after which it became a wool-scouring company's office into the 1950s.
s: 1899 gold-boom bank building in the West End
_facts: Built 1899 for the Bank of New South Wales
Federation Free Classical stone-and-brick building on the corner of Cliff Street
Bank of NSW operated here until 1926; then the Swan Wool Scouring Company's office until the 1950s

w: Fremantle's first Presbyterian church, built at 90 South Terrace on the corner with Parry Street. It's one of only six Presbyterian churches nationally that chose to stay independent rather than join the Uniting Church.
s: Fremantle's first Presbyterian church, still independent
_facts: First Presbyterian church built in Fremantle
Located at 90 South Terrace, on the corner of Parry Street
One of only six Presbyterian churches that declined to join the Uniting Church

w: A West End heritage building on Mouat Street dating from Fremantle's gold-rush boom, once home to the German Consulate and the Norddeutscher-Lloyd shipping line's offices. It later traded as the Tarantella Night Club, the name it's still known by today.
s: Old German Consulate building, later a nightclub
_facts: Also known as the German Consulate and Norddeutscher-Lloyd Building
Dates from the late 19th/early 20th-century gold-rush boom
Located on Mouat Street in the Fremantle West End Heritage area

w: Known in Noongar as Mudurup, one of WA's most iconic beaches - sheltered by offshore reefs, drawing around 600,000 visitors a year. The 1996 Indiana Tea House on the foreshore is an internationally recognised landmark. Hosts the Rottnest Channel Swim and Sculpture by the Sea, heritage-listed since 2005.
s: Iconic sheltered beach, home to the Indiana Tea House
_facts: Noongar name Mudurup
Heritage-listed since 2005; around 600,000 visitors a year
1996 Indiana Tea House is an internationally recognised landmark
Hosts the Rottnest Channel Swim and Sculpture by the Sea

w: A small rise overlooking the port city, known to the Whadjuk people as Dwerda Weelardinup - 'place of the dingo spirit' - with the peak itself called Walyarup, 'sea eagle nest'. Since the early 1900s it's been controlled by the Department of Defence and built up with military buildings.
s: A hill over the port, once 'sea eagle nest'
_facts: Whadjuk name Dwerda Weelardinup ('place of the dingo spirit'); peak called Walyarup ('sea eagle nest')
Used for military purposes since the early 1900s under the Department of Defence
